title: Simultaneous estimation of relative phase and coherence in astronomical interferometry
authors: Yawen Tang, Wei Ye, Lu Qin, Jinxin Li, Xinxin Wang, Zunlue Zhu, Shoukang Chang, Shao-Ming Fei, Xingdong Zhao
abstract: Astronomical interferometry is a cornerstone technique for high-resolution stellar imaging and observational astrophysics, extracting spatial information from the coherence of light collected by separated telescopes. Since the degree of coherence is complex, a genuine imaging task requires the joint recovery of the modulus and the relative phase, instead of independent singleparameter estimations. We investigate the simultaneous estimation of both parameters based on direct interferometry scheme and continuou-svariable quantum teleportation scheme. We find that in simultaneous estimation the direct interferometry scheme consistently yields a lower quantum Cramér-Rao bound, demonstrating its superiority over the continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme. Furthermore, we establish the conditions under which the classical Cramér-Rao bound for Gaussian measurements saturates the quantum Cramér-Rao bound, identifying heterodyne detection as a near-optimal measurement scheme in the large mean photon number regime. An analysis of transmission loss reveals that the direct interferometry scheme yields superior precision in the short-baseline regime, whereas the continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme outperforms it at longer baselines.
summary: This paper theoretically investigates how best to estimate both the phase and coherence of light collected by astronomical interferometers. It compares two methods—direct measurement versus quantum teleportation—and finds that direct interferometry is generally superior, though the optimal method depends on the baseline length. The work establishes key theoretical bounds for achievable estimation precision.
main_problem: The core problem is the simultaneous estimation of both the relative phase ($\phi$) and the degree of coherence ($\mu$ or $\gamma$) in astronomical interferometry, as joint recovery is necessary for true imaging.
main_result: The direct interferometry scheme consistently achieves a lower Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB) compared to the continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme. Furthermore, performance depends on baseline length: direct methods are better for short baselines, while teleportation excels at long baselines.
method: The analysis uses Gaussian multiparameter quantum estimation theory, comparing the Classical and Quantum Fisher Information Matrices (CRB vs QCRB) derived for two distinct measurement schemes.
model_or_system: The physical system is astronomical interferometry using separated telescopes to measure light coherence. The theoretical models compared are the direct interferometry scheme and a continuous-variable quantum teleportation scheme utilizing squeezed vacuum states.
key_observables: Relative phase ($\phi$), degree of coherence ($\gamma$ or $\mu$), Quantum Cramér-Rao Bound (QCRB), and Classical Cramér-Rao Bound (CRB).
important_parameters: Total mean photon number ($\epsilon$), transmissivity ($T$), baseline length ($L$), and the coherence parameter ($\gamma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on Gaussian measurement theory, and specific comparisons are made under assumptions regarding transmission loss coefficients.
figures_summary: Figures compare QCRB vs. photon number ($\epsilon$) for different coherences ($\gamma$); they also plot the optimized difference between CRB and QCRB, and show a crossover behavior in performance versus baseline length ($L$).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the joint estimation problem, develops theoretical frameworks for both direct interferometry and quantum teleportation schemes using Fisher information matrices, derives and compare the resulting QCRBs, and finally analyzes the dependence of precision on environmental factors like transmission loss and baseline distance.
why_interesting: This work directly applies advanced quantum estimation theory to a fundamental problem in astrophysics (interferometry), providing quantitative comparisons between different quantum measurement protocols for parameter estimation.
